headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage: OpenHands can write/browse a runtime sandbox while transformers reads/writes files and serves pipelines.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write files in a Docker runtime and use MCP, while transformers reads Python/model/example files and exposes stdin/stdout and serve-style APIs. A shared mounted volume or file handoff lets attacker-controlled content from one agent be parsed by the other as instructions. The pathway is plausible in default pair deployments, though not inherently guaranteed.
conditions: IF the two agents share a mounted workspace or exchanged files are treated as instructions
IF OpenHands forwards file content through MCP or browser output into transformers prompts
mitigations: Disable MCP bridges between the agents
Require explicit human review before copying outputs
Prefix all inter-agent files as untrusted data
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and can egress broadly; transformers also reads and writes local files and can call Hugging Face Hub or serve APIs. If they share a workspace, sensitive file contents can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs or outbound requests. The profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary between them.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted directory
IF either agent is given secrets or regulated documents in that directory
mitigations: Block outbound network for the file-processing agent
Review logs for copied file contents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent DLP and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. OpenHands also modifies git state, so concurrent edits to the same repo or workspace can overwrite each other or corrupt state without locking. This is a default-dangerous overlap because neither profile shows coordination primitives or locking.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git repository
IF they run concurrently without an external lock or scheduler
mitigations: Serialize write access with a lock file
Disable git writes for one agent

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate shell/browser-driven outputs, and transformers can consume files or pipeline inputs and emit downstream artifacts. If transformers treats OpenHands output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect documents or code. The profiles show no built-in verification step between them, but they also do not prove automatic action-taking, so medium fits.
conditions: IF transformers ingests OpenHands-produced text without validation
IF downstream scripts or documents are generated directly from that output
mitigations: requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands explicitly handles model provider API keys and files in its runtime, while transformers processes text, audio, images, video, and multimodal data. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is visible: sensitive runtime files could be exposed if both agents share data. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling of the same data class.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared runtime files
IF logs or outputs retain that data beyond intended use
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
